props.title: Late May and June, on everybody’s calendar at once.

props.html: Graduation parties land in a three-week window at the end of May and the start of June, on the same weekends as every other graduation in the district and the first wedding Saturdays of the summer, so the date is the thing to send early. A college graduation runs a couple of weeks ahead of the high schools, and the Sunday afternoon after a Saturday ceremony is the easier ask on both calendars.

props._notes: The graduation calendar from the host's side: late May and June, the same weekends as every other graduation in the district and the June weddings, and the afternoon-into-evening shape. Calendar facts only, no clock times.

props.title: Graduation party entertainment ideas.
props.lede: The graduate’s friends and the graduate’s grandparents want different music, and the size that suits the party is the one that can play both.

rows.term: A singer taking the graduate’s requests
rows.text: One voice and a guitar playing the songs the whole family knows while the food is on, then the ones the graduate asked for once the table thins out. Tejas Singh builds requests live with a looper, and the same booking grows to a quartet if the lawn turns into a floor.

rows.term: A jazz duo for the family lunch
rows.text: Upright bass and guitar under a long table, for the graduation that’s a lunch for the grandparents first. The jazz duo plays it.

rows.term: A DJ set built from the graduate’s playlist
rows.text: Hand us the playlist and the DJ builds the afternoon around it, then carries the late end of the party indoors.

rows.term: A party band, or live band karaoke
rows.text: A trio or a quartet for a party big enough to have a floor, which Tony Medina plays up to a four piece. Live band karaoke gets the friends and the parents singing in the same hour, because its book runs from the 80s onward.
The song a parent wants played for their kid in front of everyone, learned for the day if it isn’t already on the song list.

items.q: Can we hire a band for a graduation party?
items.a: Yes. Most graduation parties book a singer with a guitar first, because one voice can play the family's songs through the food and the graduate's once the table thins out. A jazz duo covers a family lunch, a DJ covers the friends, and live band karaoke gets both generations singing. It's one contract with one personal contact, booked through Signet Artists in Denver.

While the food is on, about as loud as the conversation at the table, so the grandparents hear each other. Once the friends have the yard, the DJ or the band plays like a party, and that loud part belongs early in the evening or indoors.

items.q: What does the yard need to provide?
items.a: A wall socket through the nearest window on a dedicated circuit, cover over the musicians and the sound gear in any forecast, and a plan for the loud part to move indoors once the light goes. A singer with a guitar or a DJ takes about 6 by 4 feet, a duo 8 by 6, a trio 12 by 8 and a quartet 14 by 10. Sets run 45 to 60 minutes with music through the breaks.

items.q: Can the musician learn one song for the graduate?
items.a: Yes. Tell us the title with the date and we can usually learn it.
